Senses.Explanation: Outside the ordinary frame of categories, grading, or established standards. Chan records apply the descriptor to sayings, phrases, actions, workings, people, and house styles, but they do not make it automatic praise. Baiyu Si contrasts phrases addressed to middle and lower capacities with handling “outside the frame” that establishes no grade of capacity. Tianyi Yihuai says a formulation is not yet a saying outside the usual frame, then contrasts it with explaining meaning by relying on scripture. Qingxu Xiujing applies the descriptor to Zhaozhou Congshen's “cypress tree in the front garden” answer. Mengtang Tan'e characterizes Yunmen Wenyan's house as solitary and steep and upheld outside the ordinary frame. Juelang Daosheng is directly asked for a phrase outside the frame and answers, “the staff-tip points out a thousand lovely peaks; before Five-Phoenix Tower, listen for good news.” Yuan'an Feng rejects Yaoshan Weiyan's own claim to possess workings outside the frame, judging that it reveals what it tries to hide. The headword occurs 1,203 times across 263 allowlisted texts.
Senses.Note: This is one corpus-wide descriptor whose application may be asserted, queried, or rejected. The allowlisted corpus does not show the modern adverbial intensifier use “especially” in the tested formations; its recurrent use here classifies something as outside an ordinary frame. Different nouns modified by the descriptor do not create different senses.

Senses.Explanation: A phrase outside the standard is a public-interview utterance class placed beyond ordinary or established standards. Yuanwu’s pointer says that if one can distinguish such a phrase, ‘raise one and understand three’; later in the same collection he says one must know the phrase outside the standard so that, when public cases and words are raised, one knows their place. An unnamed questioner can ask directly, ‘what is a phrase outside the standard?’ and receive the answer, ‘the staff-tip points out a thousand peaks; before the Five-Phoenix Tower, listen for fine news.’ Other speakers coordinate it with ‘the upward pivot,’ contrast it with ‘the basic-function mechanism,’ or attribute it to Yunmen while saying that Yunmen and the Buddha each displayed their own style but had not yet accorded with the basis. One later discourse dismisses ‘the phrase outside the standard’ as a worn-out straw sandal alongside ‘the upward pivot’ as rotten hemp rope. Zen usage therefore bends the ordinary ‘outside the norm’ modifier into a technical phrase-class that masters request, distinguish, perform, compare with other phrase and mechanism classes, and appraise in public interviews.

Senses.Explanation: A ghost cave is a dark, dead enclosure in which someone settles and tries to make a livelihood. Chan speakers bend the literal cave into a verdict on being trapped in blank stillness, fixed understanding, or the very attempt to lodge in neither coming nor going. Dahui Zonggao applies it to students who suppress movement and then sit unable to turn; other commentators say a formulation leads people into 'making a livelihood in a ghost cave.' The phrase condemns an enclosed dead end—it does not name a productive retreat.

Senses.Explanation: The phrase pictures an enclosed ghost cave in which the records place calculation, immobile sitting, and attempted livelihood. The corpus repeatedly extends it as 'making a living inside a ghost cave' (鬼窟裏作活計, 164 occurrences), 'sitting inside a ghost cave' (鬼窟裏坐, 17), and 'inside a ghost cave beneath the black mountain' (黑山下鬼窟裏, 15). Dahui warns, 'take special care not to reckon inside a ghost cave' (切忌向鬼窟裏卜度), elsewhere describes remaining motionless inside a ghost cave below the black mountain, and in a separate public-address work says that when stillness does not become present, 'there is a phenomenon outside the mind: sitting inside a ghost cave, unable to move' (既不現前則心外有法坐在鬼窟裏不能轉動). Yuanwu writes that activity based on conscious calculation is 'making a living inside a ghost cave' and repeats the wording after 'as soon as you calculate' (纔作計較). Yunmen's record sets up a conditional choice: if the cited participant cannot answer, he is 'sitting inside a ghost cave.' These are the corpus's own spatial and verbal extensions of the image; the texts do not supply a separate object-definition for the cave.
